chapter_theme: Akananuru 341 to 360, from the நித்திலக்கோவை section: paalai partings dominate, with heroines blessing or reproaching the man who left for wealth and the hero arguing with his heart on the road and at home, set among kurinji and neythal poems of secret meetings pressing toward marriage, two mullai homecomings and one marutham refusal; puram names (Cheralathan, Nannan, Anji, Pulli, Killi Valavan at Koodal) recur as measures of fame, noise and giving.

341.reading: The heroine tells her friend there is no way through: the kongu has leaves fit to pluck, the koel calls from the mango, and on the Kaveri's sand after the flood has fallen the bull drinks with his cow and sleeps with her under the kaanji's falling pollen; this rich season is for those who have their partner beside them.
341.nuance: The last line turns the whole riverside scene into a list of what she lacks: every couple in it, animal and human, has a companion to enjoy the season with. The season's signs are spring's, so the poem implies that he had promised to be back by now.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman left behind laments the season she must spend alone

comparisons.tenor: the dark streaks of the river sand after the flood

iraicchi.act: the bull drinks with his cow and they lie down together to sleep on the sand
iraicchi.sense: even the cattle spend the season with their mates, while her husband stays away

342.reading: The hero rebukes his heart, which neither stops when checked nor stays when held: am I not your kinsman? Cherish me as if we had already embraced; she is harder to reach than the mountain goddesses hidden in the rock caves of the untouched waterfall, in the land of the victorious Pandya, while I cannot lie on her lovely waist.
342.nuance: The long middle (lines 4 to 11) praises the Pandya, called தென்னன் and of the கவுரியர் line, as the destroyer of a cattle-raiders' stronghold; it serves only to place the cave of the hill goddesses, the image of a woman out of reach. The poem is the hero's half of the kalavu when the friend has said no.

colophon.thurai: அல்ல குறிப்பிட்ட தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover longing for an embrace not yet granted

comparisons.tenor: how the heart should treat the hero

occasion.words: அல்ல குறிப்பிட்ட தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

343.reading: On the road for wealth, the hero tells his heart, which wants to turn back to the girl with shoulders like bamboo, that it has taken up a high endeavour and should not now look back: the path runs past a hero-stone whose top was chipped by the salt-carriers' cart wheels, its garland withered and its letters worn, through a forest where under the yaa's shade the salt-traders unload their donkeys.
343.nuance: The hero-stone with its worn inscription, which travellers use for another purpose (வேறுபயம்), is part of what the heart must pass: the dead are marks on a trade road. Lines 13 and 14 (the traders' load and the companion in distress) are compressed and their construction is not certain.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் இடைச்சுரத்து மீளக் கருதிய நெஞ்சினைக் கழறிப்போயது.

thinai_evidence.note: the glaring forked paths of the forest and the passing sun

comparisons.tenor: the shade of the yaa tree

344.reading: His task done, the hero tells his charioteer to drive fast, bells ringing and horses leaping, through the forest where rain has fallen on the white saline ground, the pidavu buds open like moonlight in the cool wind and peacocks gather, so that before evening falls his beloved, worn with the pallor of longing, may show a smiling face.
344.nuance: The rain season has come, which is the time he promised, so speed is a matter of keeping his word as much as of desire. The peacocks are compared to something the bright-browed women make or play with (கைமாண் தோணி), and that object is not clear.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-soaked forest and the pidavu of the rainy season

345.reading: The heroine tells her friend that he promised to go only when rain had cooled the land, and to spend a few days first with her wearing vengai garlands from Ezhil hill, which a famous poet sang; though he has broken that word, she wishes his road well: may the forest grow lovely with nunavu flowers on the red sand path and trees putting out dark shoots for his young spearmen to wear, and may they rest in the itti's shade.
345.nuance: Complaint turns to blessing in the middle of the poem: she names his lie and in the same breath prays that the road be cool for him. Ezhil hill is fixed by its fame in song (a poet given horses by the grace of the forest goddess), so a place in praise poetry measures her lost happiness.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has gone on the dry road before the promised season

346.reading: The friend turns the husband away with a laugh: lord of the town where the heron, its back like wet plaster, waits watching the overflow of the dam the toddy-glad farmers built of kaanji stakes, sugarcane and sod, eyeing the silver kayal fish, we no longer care; the day you went to her house with your lute-player, drum and drinking friends, that bangled girl rejoiced more than the Chera with the kothai garland when Pazhaiyan Maran routed Killi Valavan's army at Koodal and seized his horses and elephants.
346.nuance: The scale of the other woman's joy is a historical defeat: a Chola camped before Madurai, beaten, his horses and elephants taken, and a third king delighting in it. The friend's mockery (நகைநன்று) frames both the heron and the victory as the rival's gains.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband went to another woman's house

ullurai.tenor: the other woman lying in wait for the husband

pairs.situation: she has marked the husband as her catch
she waits patiently for him to come within reach
she profits from a household others laboured to build

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the heron and fish of the marutham field in a marutham poem without leaving its land (porul 7.27)

347.reading: The heroine tells her friend that though he left her, with her shoulders losing their old beauty, pallor eating her looks and the harsh street's gossip loud as the drum of Cheralathan who drove back the sea and cut the kadambu, may his work succeed; he has crossed the mountains where, after a tiger's leap, a young cow-elephant frightened by the tusker's roar has lost her calf and searches with her trunk on her head like a woman who has lost her child.
347.nuance: The blessing (வாய்க்கதில்) is spoken in the middle of her own wasting. The cow-elephant searching like a bereaved mother is a picture of the road's terror, and also of a loss being searched for, which is her own state.

thinai_evidence.note: the rainless slope where bamboo withers

comparisons.tenor: the cow-elephant searching for her calf

348.reading: With the lover listening, the heroine asks what will become of her heart, which trusted the fine but unstable words of the lord of the land where the hill folk drink toddy of jackfruit and honey matured in bamboo, offer it to the god's high peak, and forget their millet field until elephants take the grain and young and old gather angrily with their bows.
348.nuance: The friend has started the talk and the heroine speaks for the man to hear: the drunken hill folk who let the field go and then rouse the whole clan are her warning of what his delay invites.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill folk and their millet field

ullurai.tenor: the lover who delays marriage while the heroine is left unguarded

pairs.situation: the lover, lost in pleasure, forgets what he promised to protect
what is left unguarded may be taken by another
her kin will be roused when the matter comes out

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the millet field she guards and its marauders, things she knows (porul 7.26)

349.reading: The heroine asks her friend what he was thinking of, letting the old beauty of the arm he bound in marriage fade, when he crossed into the land of strange speech, through the country of Nannan, whose word is true as a balance beam and who gives the spoils of broken forts unasked to weary bards, where on the beautiful hill a tusker that has eaten flame-red vengai rests its tired trunk on its brow like a snake climbing a rock.
349.nuance: வரைந்துதாம் பிணித்த says it was he who bound her arm in marriage, so the loss is a broken undertaking, not only a sorrow. Nannan's unhesitating giving stands against the husband who left to get wealth.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband has crossed the wasteland into a land of foreign speech

comparisons.tenor: the mouthful of red vengai flowers
the tusker's trunk resting on its brow

350.reading: To the lover leaving after a daytime meeting, the friend says the backwater's flowers are closing with the tide, the ford is silent with no one passing and the crab gone from its burrow: do not yoke your mules to the chariot, but for her sake stay and then go; see, there is our little town, on the long sandbank where the fishermen who dive for conch come in to Korkai's welcome, blowing their shells.
350.nuance: Pointing to her own town at dusk is an invitation to stay and also a hint to come openly to the village, which is how the friend nudges the lover toward marriage.

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறி வந்து நீங்குந் தலைமகற்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater at the hour the flowers close

occasion.words: பகற்குறி வந்து நீங்குந் தலைமகற்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது

351.reading: Returning with wealth won abroad, the hero asks his heart whether she knows yet that his task is done: she who counts each day the marks drawn on the wall for the days he set, with tears falling on her gold earring, chin on her hand on the bed, worshipping the bird omens, may hear at her ear the lizard that chirps whenever she thinks of him, as a medicine for her aching shoulders.
351.nuance: The man imagines the woman's waiting in close detail, the tally marks, the omens of bird and lizard, so that what he hopes to bring home is the end of a routine he knows she keeps.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்முற்றி மறுத்தராநின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the sun-scorched scrub path

occasion.words: பொருள்முற்றி மறுத்தராநின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

352.reading: The bride tells her friend that she spoke well and truly in praising the hill lord, where the male monkey clasps a pot-sized jackfruit as a drummer clasps his drum behind a dancing girl, with a dancing peacock before him, and calls to his sweet mate by the waterfall, as a man of good family who would not leave her nor speak falsely: the friend is sweeter to her than the new mode the bard composed for Anji's famous song, and sweeter even than the wedding day.
352.nuance: The friend's earlier speech is quoted, with its own scene of the monkey keeping its mate, so the poem confirms after the wedding what the go-between promised before it. The second alternative of the colophon puts the speech before the wedding, when it is only arranged.

colophon.thurai: வரைந்து எய்திய பின்றை மணமனைக்கட் சென்ற தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது. வரைவு மலிந்து சொல்லிய தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the monkey, waterfall and hill lord

comparisons.tenor: the monkey clasping the jackfruit behind the dancing peacock
the friend's sweetness to the bride

occasion.words: வரைந்து எய்திய பின்றை மணமனைக்கட் சென்ற தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது
வரைவு மலிந்து சொல்லிய தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியதூஉமாம்

iraicchi.act: the male monkey gathers the ripe jackfruit in his arms and calls his sweet mate to share it
iraicchi.sense: the hill lord, like the monkey of his hill, keeps the one he has joined and does not leave her

353.reading: Home again with wealth, the hero answers his heart, which urges a second journey: the days of waking life pass like a dream, age comes, and love's rare joy has its season; even if you do not see this, will you not think, crossing the treeless summer waste where a stag embraces his drooping doe and both turn from the leaves for want of water at a dried pond, of the virtue of the long-haired woman who tends weary guests in our cool hall and speaks sweetly with us in bed?
353.nuance: The argument against going is made from impermanence: time and age are reasons to stay with love and household, not to renounce it. Her virtue is defined by the guests she feeds, so the home he would leave is a place of giving.

colophon.thurai: முன்னொரு காலத்துப் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்த தலைமகன் பொருண்முற்றி வந்திருந்த காலத்து மீண்டும் பொருள் கடாவின நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hot summer waste

iraicchi.act: the stag holds close his weary doe and stays with her in thirst at the dried pond
iraicchi.sense: even the stag keeps by his mate in hardship, so the man should not leave his wife again for wealth

354.reading: The attendants tell the hero, his work done: the king has won and raised his flag in the camp where elephants clashed, cows frisk with their calves in every grove and herdsmen raise their flutes; if you would enter home in the joy of victory, sandal dust on your gold-garlanded chest that poets praise, where then will the pallor go from the brow of your faultless lady with flower-like eyes?
354.nuance: The victory and the cowherds' evening are both reasons to go now; the question at the end means her pallor will vanish the moment he arrives.

thinai_evidence.note: herdsmen and milch cows in the groves

thurai_akam.speaker: pira
thurai_akam.note: the speakers are the hero's attendants (உழையர்)

355.reading: Told that he is going, the heroine answers her friend: when spring comes of itself, when the mango puts out shoots, the koel calls and bees hum on the budding branch like the strings of a paalai lute touched by a master, the season in which lovers forget their rich homes in cool groves, let us go and show him the loosened bangles, quarrel with him and come back, saying: while we are alone, you who love gold and have no grace have become like this.
355.nuance: She rehearses her reproach before he has gone, and the reproach is about the season: he will be away in the time made for lovers. The paalai lute in the simile names the very mode of parting.

thinai_evidence.note: she is to be left alone while he goes for gold

356.reading: The friend tells the heroine how the lord of the town, where the tortoise at the lower ford drinks the washing water and rolls like a kinai drum with the water-hen as its player, saw me in the long street and seized my gold-bangled arm; I cried 'Mother!' and he let go, and since then, so as not to betray our old affection, I have kept a tongue like stone glued with lac and told our mother nothing; even if he showed us no grace and killed, the killing would be no fault: so what is your mind, you with hair like Nannan's cane?
356.nuance: The friend tells of her own encounter as a test: she has been seized and stayed silent, and she now asks the heroine to accept the man's suit. Lines 11 to 17, with the Chola lord of Vallam and the enemies at the door, are obscure in our text.

colophon.thurai: பின்னின்ற தலைமகற்குக் குறைநேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகளைக் குறை நயப்பக் கூறியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a suitor seeking the girl's consent, before marriage

occasion.words: பின்னின்ற தலைமகற்குக் குறைநேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகளைக் குறை நயப்பக் கூறியது

357.reading: The friend comforts the heroine: though he has crossed the great forest of Umbar, where a tiger kills a tusker to end the weakness of his hungry mate and rolls on the reddened rock, and the elephant herd turns back holding each other's trunks, he will not stay away without thinking of your shoulders; he will be kind, remembering your glance, like a blue lily swaying in the wind on a rain-filled pond.
357.nuance: The tiger's kill is violent, but what it does is provide for a mate weak with pregnancy; that is the reassurance, as the colophon's வற்புறீஇயது expects.

thinai_evidence.note: the great forest he crossed

iraicchi.act: the tiger kills an elephant to end the hunger of his pregnant mate
iraicchi.sense: as the tiger toils for his mate, the man is away working for her and will come back to her

358.reading: By day, with the lover hidden nearby, the friend tells the heroine that she no longer plays with her companions in the deep spring, hair dressed with cool kuvalai, graceful as a blue-necked peacock dancing; if mother sees her changed colour and asks, what can the friend say of the sickness given by the lord of the high hill, where the long white waterfall looks like a flag on a war elephant?
358.nuance: The question is meant for the man to hear: the mother has noticed, and only marriage can answer her. The waterfall like a flag on an elephant is the hill lord's own country turned into a banner.

thinai_evidence.note: the great hill, spring and waterfall

359.reading: The friend asks the heroine why she is helpless, saying he has stayed away not knowing how she hides her tearful eyes and pale shoulders: he has taken their beauty with him, rich as the Chera's Veliyam, on the mountain road of Pulli, where an elephant that has lost its beloved mate trumpets back to the clouds like the music of travelling players on a great rock, and smoke from burning fields mingles with waterfall spray.
359.nuance: Her beauty is not lost but carried off, held by him on the road; the friend reframes the wasting as a trust he holds. The elephant's cry for its lost mate shows that the road itself mourns a separation.

thinai_evidence.note: he is delayed on the hard road

iraicchi.act: the elephant that has lost its beloved mate trumpets for her on the slope
iraicchi.sense: the man on that road, parted as the elephant is, feels the loss too and will turn back

360.reading: Refusing a daytime meeting, the friend tells the lover that after the day spent in the flowering grove, when the sun goes behind the western hill, bees leave the neythal and sky and sea at dusk take on the joined form of the two great gods, his going leaves her desolate; so let him come at night, keeping his trained horse from neighing while the town sleeps, leaving the chariot far off and crossing the sand softly like an elephant coming down a hill, to their trysting place in the punnai grove where the anril roosts on the palm.
360.nuance: The friend's detailed instructions for secrecy (the muffled horse, the chariot left behind) show how dangerous the night tryst is, which is also an argument for marriage. The two gods of the simile are not named; the sky and sea joined suggest two figures of different colour.

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறி வந்த தலைமகற்குத் தோழி பகற்குறி மறுத்து இரவுக் கறி நேர்ந்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore at sunset

comparisons.vehicle: இருபெரும் தெய்வத்து உருவுடன் இயைந்த தோற்றம் போல
comparisons.tenor: the evening sky joined to the sea

links.note: Both are mullai poems in which the hero, his work done, tells the charioteer to drive fast through the rain-fed forest to his waiting wife.
links.teaches: Akananuru 34 grounds the hurry in an animal pair (the stag feeding and guarding his doe) while 344 grounds it in the clock, before evening falls, so the homecoming formula could be driven either by an emblem of care or by the promised hour.

links.note: Both are mullai homecomings after the task: in 344 the hero urges his charioteer; in 354 the attendants urge the hero, naming the victory and the cowherds' evening.
links.teaches: The pair shows the same return from both ends of command: the hero who orders speed in 344 is himself ordered by his men in 354, and both make the wife's pallor the thing his arrival cures.

links.note: Both poems by Mamoolanar use Cheralathan, who drove back the sea and cut the kadambu: 127 his tribute treasure, 347 his drum.
links.teaches: One poet drew two different measures from a single Chera victory, its plunder as the scale of the wealth the husband will not stay for and its drum as the scale of the gossip's noise, so akam borrowed puram events for value and for loudness alike.

links.note: Both paalai poems pass through the country of Ezhil hill: 345 recalls it as the hill sung by a poet given horses, 349 as Nannan's land where bards are given wealth unasked.
links.teaches: Read together they show that Ezhil hill was known through its patron's gifts to poets, so the absent husband's road ran through a landscape whose fame was generosity, sharpening the contrast with the man who left home to get wealth.

links.note: The Kural's woman has worn her fingers marking the days since he left; 351 names the marks drawn on the wall that she counts each day.
links.teaches: The couplet speaks only from the woman's side, while 351 puts the same tally marks in the returning man's mind, so the counting of days on the wall was a known practice that both partners could picture, not a private secret of the one who waits.

links.note: Both start from the coming of age: the Naladiyar's wise renounce early because grey hair will come; 353's hero refuses to leave his wife because the days pass like a dream and age is coming.
links.teaches: The same premise, that youth is short, yields opposite counsels, renunciation in the Naladiyar and staying in married love in 353, so impermanence was a shared starting point that the akam poets turned toward the household and the didactic poets away from it.

links.note: Both are spoken by the hero to his heart about the journey for wealth: 351 as he returns with it, 353 when the heart at home urges a second journey.
links.teaches: Placed in sequence the two show the pull of wealth outlasting its success: the heart that raced home in 351 is restless again in 353, and only the argument from age and the wife's virtue holds it back.

links.note: Both are the man at the king's war: the couplet wishes the king victory so that he may join his wife for the evening feast; in 354 the king has won and raised his flag, and the attendants urge the hero home before her pallor deepens.
links.teaches: The couplet's wish has two conditions, the king's victory and the evening at home, and 354 shows them met in order (the flag raised, the herds coming in at dusk), so the Kural's line compresses a whole mullai homecoming whose hinge is that the hero's private return waits on the public war.

links.note: Purananuru 92 is Avvai's song to Anji calling her words a child's babble he graciously hears; 352 measures the friend's sweetness against a famous bard's new tune for Anji's praise.
links.teaches: The praise songs for Anji, which Avvai offers modestly as babble, had become in akam a byword for sweetness, showing that puram performances were known to the love poets' audience as celebrated pieces of music.

links.note: Both are neythal poems in which the friend answers a lover's daytime visit at dusk: 350 asks him to stay and points to the town, 360 refuses the day meeting and sets a secret night one.
links.teaches: At the same hour the friend has two opposite tactics, drawing the lover openly toward the village in 350 and hiding him by night in 360, so the dusk scene of neythal could press either toward marriage or toward deeper secrecy.

links.note: Both open on the spring signs of new leaves and the koel calling in the mango and set them against the man's absence.
links.teaches: The same signs bring helpless lament in 341 ('there is no way through') and a planned reproach in 355 (we will go and quarrel with him), so the season's cue fixed the occasion but not the heroine's response.

new_concepts.gloss: marriage as the end of secret love; the friend's pressing of the lover to marry (வரைவு கடாயது)
new_concepts.label_source: the colophons' word (வரைவு கடாயது); the verses imply it

new_concepts.gloss: the appointed meeting place of secret lovers, by day (பகற்குறி) or by night (இரவுக்குறி)
new_concepts.label_source: the colophons' word; the verses name day and night meetings

source_issues: akananuru:341: the flag reports 13 lines in our base text against 12 in the commentary edition (pmuni0534); the poem reads complete as it stands, but the lineation differs.
akananuru:347: line 16 is repeated as line 24 of akananuru:389 (flag); both poems are Mamoolanar's, so it may be the poet's own formula rather than a copying error.
akananuru:348: the colophon thurai has a stray footnote numeral, '1சிறைப்புறத்தானாக'; copied as is in `colophon`.
akananuru:358: the colophon thurai has தலைமட்குச் for தலைமகட்குச்; copied as is in `colophon`. Line 2 is repeated as line 5 of akananuru:378 (flag).
akananuru:359: lineation flag: a printed line number 5 stands on line 10; the base text has 16 lines against 15 in the commentary edition (pmuni0534).
akananuru:360: the colophon thurai has இரவுக் கறி for இரவுக் குறி; copied as is in `colophon`.
akananuru:344: line 3 has முடககாற் for the expected முடக்காற் (a missing pulli).
akananuru:356: lines 11 to 17 (the Chola lord of Vallam, the enemies at the door) do not construe clearly in our text; the reading there is uncertain.
